name: Anti-clericalism
summary: Anti-clericalism opposes the political, economic and educational power of religious institutions and clergy, historically mostly the Catholic Church. Its programme is to separate church and state, remove clergy from schools and public office, and curb or confiscate church property, while usually guaranteeing individual freedom of conscience. It is a stance on clerical authority rather than a full programme on economics or other issues, and it has coexisted with liberal, radical and socialist politics.
scope: The republican and liberal anti-clericalism of France (Revolution, Ferry laws of 1881-82, Combes and the 1905 separation law), with parallels in Spain, Mexico, Italy and Germany's Kulturkampf. It excludes militant atheist state campaigns, which are treated as a separate strand, and most answers outside church-state, education and clerical authority are inferred and low confidence.

keyFigures.name: Emile Combes

keyFigures.name: Benito Juarez

universal-healthcare.rationale: Anti-clericalism concerns clerical power, not economic policy; adherents ranged from liberals to socialists, and the one link is that church-run charity was often taken over by the state.

raise-minimum-wage.rationale: Wage policy lay outside the movement's concern with clergy; its supporters spanned liberal, radical and socialist parties.

markets-allocate-better.rationale: Nothing in opposition to clerical authority settles the market question; Liberal reformers and the socialist left both took part.

public-ownership.rationale: Adherents split by party on public ownership; the shared cause concerned church influence, though seizing church property was a common measure.

tax-the-wealthy.rationale: No stance on taxation is part of the doctrine; it is a clergy-focused politics shared across economic camps.

unions-good.rationale: Unions were not the movement's subject; Spanish republicans and French radicals differed on labor questions.

property-fundamental.rationale: Anti-clerical governments repeatedly nationalised church property (Mendizabal, Juarez, 1905 inventories), so property is not treated as untouchable, at least where the church holds it.

regulate-corporations.rationale: Business regulation was not an anti-clerical issue and adherents differed.

cut-welfare.rationale: No doctrine on welfare; the movement's one link is that it moved charity and schooling from church to state.

worker-ownership.rationale: Cooperative ownership was a matter for socialists and anarchists within the wider movement, not a core anti-clerical claim.

surveillance-ok.rationale: Mixed: the Combes government's use of Masonic lodges to monitor officers' religion (the Fiches affair) shows willingness, yet it caused a backlash and liberal adherents objected.

legalize-drugs.rationale: Unrelated to clerical power; no recorded position.

restrict-hate-speech.rationale: The 1905 law punished clergy who defamed officials or urged resistance to law from the pulpit, yet it protects free expression generally, and general hate-speech law was not at issue.

strong-leader.rationale: Anti-clerical movements were mostly republican and parliamentary, though some were led by strong executives such as Juarez or Calles; inferred as leaning against personal rule.

state-harmful.rationale: Anti-clerics want a strong civil state to curb the church, nationalise property and run schools, so they reject the idea that the state is harmful.

limit-guns.rationale: No stance; not an issue for the movement.

empower-police-military.rationale: Not a defining question; anti-clerical governments used force against the church (Calles, Spain) but liberal adherents did not seek a general expansion.

legalize-sex-work.rationale: No documented position; liberal and puritan strands differ.

decide-locally.rationale: The movement relied on national law (Ferry laws, 1905 law) to override local clerical control, so inferred mild disagreement.

rehabilitation.rationale: Penal philosophy was not part of the movement; Combes-era and Calles-era governments jailed clergy, but no general view on punishment follows.

traditional-family.rationale: The church is the usual defender of traditional family structures, and anti-clericals resisted its authority over marriage, though they were not uniformly against the family.

same-sex-marriage.rationale: Not a historical issue; modern anti-clericals see religious doctrine as an illegitimate basis for marriage law, so inferred agreement.

abortion-legal.rationale: Inferred: opposition to church influence over law leads modern adherents to resist religious limits on abortion, though historical anti-clerics did not address it.

more-religion-public.rationale: Reducing religion's role in public life and clerical influence on politics is the defining aim.

correct-racial-injustice.rationale: Racial redress was not an issue for the classic movement, and sources record no stance.

gender-social-construct.rationale: Gender theory is unrelated to anti-clerical politics, so no position can be sourced.

preserve-national-culture.rationale: Split: nationalists such as Garibaldi and Bismarck saw the church as foreign, while liberals did not centre national culture.

gradual-change.rationale: Anti-clerics often pushed rapid confiscations and secularising laws against entrenched church institutions, though parliamentary republicans moved by statute.

reduce-immigration.rationale: Immigration levels were not part of the anti-clerical agenda, and the sources record no position among adherents.

empower-international-orgs.rationale: Not addressed; the Holy See as a foreign power was a target, but that is not about international bodies generally.

free-trade.rationale: Trade policy was never an anti-clerical matter, and adherents differed by party.

nation-first.rationale: Not addressed beyond the claim that the church answers to a foreign authority.

humanitarian-intervention.rationale: Anti-clericalism says nothing on foreign military intervention; adherents differed by party.

open-borders.rationale: Border policy never entered anti-clerical programmes, so no stance can be sourced.

limit-growth.rationale: No position; modernity and progress were generally favoured.

drastic-climate-action.rationale: Climate policy is anachronistic for the classic movement and is not tied to church-state conflict.

tech-solves-problems.rationale: Progress and science were opposed to clerical obscurantism in Latin American and French rhetoric, so a mild inferred agreement.

expand-nuclear.rationale: Nuclear power postdates the classic movement and has no link to church-state conflict.

revolution-justified.rationale: Revolutionary France, Mexico and Republican Spain used revolutionary or extra-parliamentary means against church power, though many liberal adherents worked by legislation.

experts-over-public.rationale: The movement centred on clerical privilege, not the balance between experts and voters; adherents were split.

central-planning.rationale: Economic planning is outside the movement; both liberal and socialist anti-clericals existed.

socialized-markets.rationale: Questions of market socialism were not raised by anti-clerical programmes and adherents split.

land-value-tax.rationale: A land tax is not tied to anti-clericalism; the movement's interest in land concerned church estates only.

tax-inheritance.rationale: Inheritance taxation was not an anti-clerical issue and adherents' views followed their wider party.

basic-income.rationale: Modern income schemes are unconnected to the church-state dispute, so the stance is neutral.

tariffs-protect-industry.rationale: Trade protection was not a clerical question; liberal and radical adherents disagreed.

state-directs-investment.rationale: Industrial policy was not an anti-clerical concern, and adherents' views followed their parties.

widespread-small-property.rationale: The movement had liberal agrarian wings that broke up church estates for wider ownership (Mendizabal sales), but no settled view.

abolish-money-wages.rationale: Only the revolutionary left among adherents wanted this; mainstream anti-clericals were liberal republicans, so inferred disagreement.

abolish-central-banks.rationale: Monetary institutions are unrelated to the movement's core, which left no recorded position.

corporatist-bargaining.rationale: Corporatism is closely tied to Catholic social teaching, which anti-clericals opposed, so inferred disagreement.

one-party-rule.rationale: Most anti-clerical movements were republican and pluralist, although Mexico and Cuba later formed single-party states.

monarchy-legitimate.rationale: Anti-clericalism tended to go with republicanism and opposition to the throne-and-altar alliance, though Joseph II was a monarch and a prominent anti-cleric.

democracy-best.rationale: The Third Republic and other anti-clerical regimes defended parliamentary republics as a protection from clerical influence, though Jacobin and Calles-era practice qualified this.

direct-votes.rationale: No position; adherents favoured representative republics.

workers-councils.rationale: Not part of the movement's republican parliamentary mainstream.

right-to-secede.rationale: Secession was not part of the movement; Italian and Spanish adherents were mostly unifying or centralising nationalists.

natural-rulers.rationale: Opposition to a privileged clerical caste implies rejection of rule by a priestly or birth elite.

political-violence-never.rationale: Revolutionary France, Mexico and Spain show violent anti-clerical action; most adherents did not forswear force, although some liberals rejected it.

war-builds-character.rationale: Glorifying war was not a doctrine of the movement; adherents had no shared view.

separate-church-state.rationale: Separation is central, as in the 1905 French law declaring that the Republic recognises, pays and subsidises no religion.

laws-from-scripture.rationale: Anti-clericals oppose religious authority in lawmaking; secular civil law replaced church control of schools, marriage and property.

private-courts-defense.rationale: The movement relies on state institutions; inferred disagreement.

military-superiority.rationale: Military rivalry is unrelated to the clerical question, and no shared position exists.

ethnic-nation.rationale: Republican anti-clericalism was civic rather than ethnic, though some nationalists used it.

class-struggle-history.rationale: Split between socialists who accepted it and liberals who did not.

equal-outcomes.rationale: Equality of outcomes was a matter for socialist adherents only; liberal anti-clericals sought equality before the law.

indigenous-land-authority.rationale: Indigenous land rights were outside the movement, though Mexican Reform liberals broke up communal and church land for individual holdings.

colonial-reparations.rationale: Reparations were not a topic for the classic anti-clerical movements, and sources record no position.

civilizational-union.rationale: Union by shared religion runs against the secular state principle.

self-interest-moral.rationale: Ethics of self-interest was not discussed by anti-clerical thinkers as part of the movement.

duties-before-rights.rationale: Liberal anticlericals stress freedom of conscience and individual rights against institutional authority.

nature-intrinsic-value.rationale: Environmental value theory is unrelated to the clerical question.

limit-population.rationale: Population limits were not part of the programme; the church's opposition to birth control is later and a secondary dispute.

industrial-civilization-disaster.rationale: Progress was opposed to clerical conservatism, so adherents rejected this.

accelerate-technology.rationale: No position; progress rhetoric but not a doctrine of acceleration.

human-enhancement.rationale: A modern bioethics issue with no tie to historic anti-clericalism; adherents would be split.

algorithmic-government.rationale: AI in government is anachronistic and unrelated to church-state conflict.

unbreakable-encryption.rationale: Digital privacy is not part of the movement; adherents' views would follow wider liberal or authoritarian leanings.

restore-past-order.rationale: The movement is progressive, aiming to end clerical privilege; clergy were opponents who sought to restore the old order.

direct-action.rationale: Mainly pursued through legislation and parliaments (1905 law, Ferry laws), though riots and expropriations also occurred.

means-match-ends.rationale: The movement used both parliamentary and forceful means against church power, so adherents were not committed to matching methods to ends.

return-to-foraging.rationale: Primitivism contradicts the movement's faith in schooling, progress and modernisation, so mild disagreement is inferred.

abolish-division-of-labor.rationale: A utopian socialist idea absent from anti-clerical programmes.

distribute-by-need.rationale: Distribution by need is a socialist doctrine; liberal anti-clericals did not adopt it and the movement as a whole is neutral.

production-for-use.rationale: Economic organisation is outside the movement's concerns.

profit-exploitation.rationale: No position; only socialist adherents would agree.

dictatorship-of-proletariat.rationale: Most anti-clericals were liberal republicans, so inferred disagreement.

collective-farming.rationale: Anti-clerical land reforms favoured breaking up church estates into private holdings, not collectivisation, but the movement has no firm stance.

capitalism-causes-war.rationale: A Marxist thesis that many liberal anti-clericals rejected, so adherents are split.

taxation-theft.rationale: Anti-clerical states relied on taxation and rejected church tithes and privileged exemptions, but taxation was not a stated concern.

harm-principle.rationale: Liberal adherents accept limits on religious practice only for public order, as in Article 1 of the 1905 law, which is close to the harm idea.

individual-rights-only.rationale: Freedom of conscience is individual, but anti-clerical states also restricted religious congregations as groups.

conscription.rationale: Compulsory military service was accepted by Third Republic France, but the movement itself has no stance on it.

exit-over-voice.rationale: Inferred from reliance on voting and legislation.

state-as-business.rationale: No position; the movement values the state as a civic institution.

positive-liberty.rationale: The movement stresses freedom from clerical coercion; whether freedom needs material means was not addressed.

media-academia-power.rationale: Anti-clericals wanted schools and universities removed from clerical control, but the claim that media and academia hold more power than elected officials is not part of their doctrine.

hereditarian-race.rationale: Rejected as inconsistent with the republican equal-citizen outlook, though not addressed historically.

organic-representation.rationale: Organic or corporatist representation is a Catholic-traditionalist idea that anti-clericals opposed.

total-state.rationale: Liberal adherents guarantee freedom of conscience, though Jacobin or Calles-style states did extend control over religion.

national-rebirth.rationale: Revolutionary regimes used rebirth rhetoric (Cult of Reason), but it is not a general view.

territorial-expansion.rationale: Expansionism was not a clerical question; Italian and revolutionary French cases were driven by other politics.

personal-loyalty-rule.rationale: Rule by personal loyalty and church-bound feudal ties belong to the order that anti-clericals attacked.

bound-labor.rationale: Bound labor was tied to church and noble estates that reformers dissolved or confiscated.

no-neutral-knowledge.rationale: Anti-clericals appealed to reason, science and secular schooling as sources of knowledge against church teaching.

universal-morality.rationale: The Ferry laws put moral and civic education in school in place of religious instruction, implying a shared secular morality, though this is not argued as doctrine.

single-common-good.rationale: Anti-clericals generally accepted pluralism through freedom of conscience, but some Jacobins and positivists sought a single rational civic morality, so the movement is divided.

jewish-state-israel.rationale: Zionism is not addressed by the movement; Jews welcomed the 1905 law as equalising their status, but no position follows.

diaspora-return-right.rationale: Not addressed by anti-clerical writing or policy.

revive-national-language.rationale: Language revival is unrelated to the movement, though Ferry's schools promoted French over regional languages and the Church's Latin.

workplace-democracy.rationale: Worker voice in company governance was left to the socialist wing; the broader movement did not address it.

school-vouchers.rationale: Anti-clericals fought public money for church schools; the Ferry laws and later measures barred congregations from teaching and removed clerical oversight.

avoid-deficit-stimulus.rationale: Fiscal policy was not a doctrine of the movement, which included both orthodox liberals and radicals.

economic-freedom.rationale: The claim linking political and economic freedom is liberal doctrine; some adherents held it while socialist ones did not.

rule-by-example.rationale: The movement wants law and secular civil authority rather than clerical moral rule.

national-self-determination.rationale: No position beyond Italian and Philippine nationalist cases.

force-without-un.rationale: The UN postdates the classic movement, and use of force abroad is not an anti-clerical issue.

reason-over-faith.rationale: Anti-clericals commonly set reason and secular schooling against clerical teaching, as in revolutionary France's Cult of Reason; but the movement targets clerical power rather than belief, and some adherents stayed believers.

welfare-for-citizens.rationale: Welfare eligibility for immigrants is unrelated to the movement's concerns.

work-for-welfare.rationale: Anti-clericals took over poor relief from church charity, but did not settle work conditions, and adherents differed.

class-collaboration.rationale: Cross-class cooperation was typical of liberal republicans but contested by socialist adherents, so the movement is split.

sacrifice-heritage.rationale: The 1905 law kept churches as historic monuments and preserved them, showing that even strong anti-clerics did not sacrifice heritage.

dominated-front.rationale: Anti-Western alignments are unrelated to anti-clericalism, and nothing in its sources addresses them.

workers-nation.rationale: Whether the working class should organise nationally or internationally was a socialist-movement dispute, not an anti-clerical one.

distinct-gender-roles.rationale: Distinct gender roles were defended by the church; Ferry-era republicans widened girls' schooling, so inferred disagreement.

ban-interest.rationale: A religious prohibition on usury; anti-clericals opposed religious limits on economic life.

racial-segregation-law.rationale: Contradicts the republican equal-citizen principle of the movement.

state-class-instrument.rationale: Marxist adherents would agree, liberals would not.

expand-fossil-fuels.rationale: Energy production was not at issue for the classic movement.

assimilate-immigrants.rationale: French republican secularism pressed assimilation to common civic norms, but the movement as a whole did not address immigration.

elite-replacement.rationale: A conspiracy claim with no place in the rationalist, republican outlook of the movement; inferred disagreement.

proportional-representation.rationale: Electoral systems varied among anti-clerical republics and no shared preference exists.

national-mission.rationale: Revolutionary France exported its anti-clerical system by conquest, yet no general doctrine of mission.

patriarchy-structural.rationale: Some republicans feared women voted as priests directed and some argued for women's education, so views split.

political-elite-corrupt.rationale: No position; clergy rather than politicians are the target.

heritable-defect-limits.rationale: Not addressed; opposed as inconsistent with liberal rights.

security-forces-accountable.rationale: Accountability for state killings is not an anti-clerical position, though the Spanish and Mexican cases involve violence by both sides.

night-watchman-state.rationale: Anti-clerics want the state to take charge of schooling, church property and religious affairs.

equal-moral-worth.rationale: Equal treatment of all religions and citizens is a republican aim of the 1905 law, which Protestants and Jews welcomed as placing them on a par with Catholics.

socialism-one-country.rationale: A debate internal to Marxism, not addressed by the anti-clerical movement.

settler-state-colonial.rationale: Settler colonialism is not discussed in anti-clerical sources, so there is no stance.

uniform-civil-code.rationale: Anti-clericals replaced church-run marriage and family law with civil law applying to all, as in the Mexican reforms and French civil legislation.

restrict-conversion.rationale: Article 1 of the 1905 law guarantees freedom of conscience and worship, which implies no restriction on conversion.

ban-cattle-slaughter.rationale: A religious rule that anti-clericals would not impose by law.

no-religion-state-schools.rationale: Secular state schooling, with clergy removed and religious instruction held outside school buildings, was the Ferry laws' central reform.

state-strengthens-encirclement.rationale: A Marxist-Leninist doctrine unrelated to the movement.

consent-of-governed.rationale: Republican anti-clericals grounded authority in civil, popular government rather than divine or clerical sanction.

trade-surplus.rationale: Mercantilist goals are not part of the anti-clerical programme.

population-transfer.rationale: Contradicts the freedom-of-conscience principle, although expulsions of orders occurred in anti-clerical states; not a stated minority policy.

initiating-force-wrong.rationale: Adherents did use force against the church in several states.

competition-drives-progress.rationale: Social Darwinist claims are not part of the movement's doctrine; adherents appealed to reason and education rather than struggle.

ban-extremist-parties.rationale: Anti-clerical states banned or dissolved religious congregations (1901 and 1904 French laws), but extremist-party bans are a different question.

freedom-as-non-domination.rationale: Opposition to arbitrary clerical power over believers fits the idea, though not stated in these terms.

separated-powers.rationale: Church and state as separate powers is central; separation of powers inside government was typical of republican adherents.

vanguard-party.rationale: Not part of the movement's liberal or republican mainstream.

priority-to-poor.rationale: No position; the church claimed this role.

right-to-buy-council-homes.rationale: A British housing policy outside the movement's scope.

restrict-strikes-picketing.rationale: Labour law was not an anti-clerical issue, and adherents followed their party lines.

population-causes-poverty.rationale: A Malthusian claim not tied to anti-clericalism.

diversity-weakens-cohesion.rationale: Republican secularism claimed to unite citizens by removing religious divisions, though not tied to ethnic diversity.

offices-by-lottery.rationale: Sortition was not proposed by anti-clerical movements, whose republics used elections.

emergency-suspend-protections.rationale: Calles and Combes governments used exceptional measures, but liberal adherents did not endorse them in principle.

price-controls-essentials.rationale: Price controls are unrelated to the clerical dispute.

party-controls-media.rationale: Liberal adherents defended a free press, though some regimes censored the church press.

party-commands-army.rationale: Republican regimes put the army under civil government.

long-naturalization-wait.rationale: Citizenship timing is not an anti-clerical issue.

representatives-worker-pay.rationale: Pay for legislators was a radical-left demand and not a general anti-clerical one.

party-discipline-binding.rationale: Party discipline was a feature of some radical blocs like the Bloc des gauches, but the movement as a whole has no doctrine about it.

pool-sovereignty.rationale: Supranational union is anachronistic for the movement and has no clerical link, though the Holy See was seen as a foreign authority.

head-commands-forces.rationale: Parliamentary republicans opposed concentration of command in an executive.

church-by-bishops.rationale: Anti-clericals reject church hierarchies' power; the 1905 law gave worship associations to lay members in parishes, weakening bishops.

clerical-rule.rationale: Rule by clergy is what the movement opposes.

defeat-own-government-war.rationale: Revolutionary defeatism was a socialist position the broader anti-clerical movement did not share and adherents divided.

unlimited-reelection.rationale: Republican norms favour limits on office.

recall-officials.rationale: Recall of officials was not an anti-clerical demand, and republics differed on it.

end-foreign-alliances.rationale: Alliances are outside the movement, and no common position exists.

abolish-rental-housing.rationale: A radical housing proposal with no link to the movement.

people-in-arms.rationale: The militia idea appeared in revolutionary France but is not a core anti-clerical claim, so the movement is neutral.

rural-life-healthier.rationale: Rural life was often seen as under clerical sway, and clergy were strongest in the countryside.

reunify-divided-nation.rationale: Italian unification against the Papal States was anti-clerical, but a general rule about divided nations is not part of the doctrine, so adherents are neutral.

educated-out-of-touch.rationale: Secular schooling and learning were valued against clerical teaching.

cultures-equal-different.rationale: Cultural relativism was not part of the movement, and some anti-clericals judged clerical societies backward, so adherents are split.

death-penalty.rationale: Anti-clerical states both executed and abolished; no shared position exists.

sex-ed-in-schools.rationale: Inferred: secular schooling under the Ferry laws removed church control of curricula, and modern adherents back sex education.

creationism-in-schools.rationale: Teaching religious doctrine in public schools is what the Ferry laws removed in favour of natural sciences.

restrict-pornography.rationale: Content restriction was historically a clerical concern, but liberal anti-clericals did not oppose pornography on principle either, leaving adherents split.

citizenship-by-descent.rationale: Nationality law is not an anti-clerical issue, and sources record no stance.

minority-language-support.rationale: Ferry's schools promoted French, while others favoured regional languages; the movement as such had no stance.

religious-exemptions.rationale: The 1905 law guaranteed worship subject only to public order, and republican secularism resists exemptions from general law.

encourage-eccentricity.rationale: J. S. Mill's view on conformity shares liberal roots with anti-clericalism, but the movement did not take it up as doctrine.

sovereign-debt-cancellation.rationale: International debt is unconnected to the clerical question.

independence-needs-economic-change.rationale: A postcolonial claim not found in anti-clerical writing.

constituent-assembly.rationale: French revolutionary and Spanish republican assemblies rewrote constitutions and church status, but not a stated doctrine.

restrict-freedoms-for-growth.rationale: Developmental authoritarianism is not part of the movement, which has no recorded position.

rich-countries-aid-poor.rationale: Global aid duties were not raised by anti-clerical movements.

independent-nuclear-deterrent.rationale: Nuclear strategy postdates the movement and is unrelated.

direct-election-head-of-state.rationale: Anti-clerical republics used both direct and parliamentary selection, so adherents are split.

central-bank-independence.rationale: Central bank design is unrelated to the clerical question.

no-land-for-peace.rationale: Territorial bargaining in the abstract is not an anti-clerical topic.

property-serves-common-good.rationale: Confiscation of church property in France, Spain and Mexico was justified as serving the public.

soviet-state-capitalist.rationale: An internal left dispute about the USSR that the movement did not address.

precautionary-principle.rationale: A modern environmental doctrine with no tie to anti-clericalism.

collective-defense.rationale: NATO-style alliance clauses are not addressed by the movement.

annexed-territory-occupation.rationale: The status of annexed land is unrelated to the clerical question, apart from the Papal States' 1870 annexation, which adherents welcomed.

subordinate-church-to-state.rationale: Curbing church property and placing clergy under civil authority is the core programme, as in the Civil Constitution of the Clergy and Mexico's Article 130.

nonpartisan-head-of-state.rationale: Republican anti-clericals often preferred a ceremonial president above parties, but others wanted a strong executive, so views are mixed.

force-to-prevent-secession.rationale: Not an anti-clerical question, though centralising liberals generally favoured national unity.

region-keeps-system.rationale: Regional autonomy arrangements are outside the movement.

sacred-ruler.rationale: Sacralising rulers is part of the throne-and-altar order that anti-clericals reject.

flat-income-tax.rationale: Tax design is unrelated to the movement, and adherents spanned the spectrum.

character-from-environment.rationale: Secular education reform assumes upbringing shapes citizens, which is a basis of Ferry's civic schooling.

sovereign-above-law.rationale: Anti-clericals opposed absolutist claims and subordinated clergy to law.

space-expansion.rationale: Space policy is anachronistic and unrelated to the movement.

mixed-constitution.rationale: Classical constitutional theory is not part of the anti-clerical programme.

results-over-ideology.rationale: Adherents varied; the movement was itself driven by principle against clerical power, and sources document no general stance on pragmatism.

leader-cult.rationale: Inferred from the movement's hostility to unquestioned authority and to quasi-religious devotion in public life; adherents wanted citizens, not subjects, so glorifying a leader sits badly with it.

equal-parenting.rationale: Anti-clericalism concerns clerical power, not family law after separation; its supporters spanned liberal, radical and socialist positions with no common view on custody.

class-struggle-under-socialism.rationale: Inferred: anti-clericalism is not a class doctrine and coexisted with liberal politics.

land-redistribution.rationale: Church estates were seized and sold in some countries, but not given to those who farm them in a program, so adherents are split.

co-ethnic-territorial-claim.rationale: Inferred: the republican strand focuses on the state within its borders.

apostasy-punishable.rationale: The 1905 law guarantees freedom of conscience and the free exercise of worship, so penalising apostasy is against it.

women-must-cover.rationale: Inferred from freedom of conscience and opposition to clerical power over individuals.

kin-peoples-union.rationale: Inferred: the strand is republican and national, not about union of kindred peoples.

national-cultural-autonomy.rationale: Inferred: the Ferry laws set up a common secular school for all, so republicans favour common over separate institutions.

rights-where-you-live.rationale: Inferred from the republican principle of equal citizenship, as in the 1905 law.

material-conditions-drive-history.rationale: Inferred: the Enlightenment and republican strand puts weight on reason and education as drivers of change.

courts-bound-by-majority.rationale: Split: republicans trusted legislatures against clerical courts, but liberals valued legal checks.

economic-self-sufficiency.rationale: Inferred: the strand has no program on trade and a republican, national frame.

armed-group-creates-revolution.rationale: Inferred: the strand worked through laws and elections, as with the Ferry and 1905 laws.

abolish-hereditary-privilege.rationale: Inferred: anti-clericalism was tied to republicanism against Church-backed monarchy and the old order.

history-own-civilization.rationale: Republican secular schooling under the Ferry laws taught civic and national history; inferred as the usual curriculum.

civilizing-tutelage.rationale: Anti-clericals were split on colonial rule (Ferry's secular republicans defended it, others opposed); the ideology has no line.

patriotic-education.rationale: Secular republican schools aimed to build citizens loyal to the republic, so civic patriotism fits, though the ideology does not define it.

end-racial-preferences.rationale: The ideology concerns clerical power, not racial preferences; supporters spanned liberal to socialist politics.

public-money-creation.rationale: Monetary policy lay outside the concerns of anti-clericalism.

capitalism-adapts.rationale: Capitalism's stability lay outside the movement's concerns; its supporters spanned liberal and socialist views.

former-empire-influence.rationale: The ideology has no foreign-influence program, and its supporters included both imperial and anti-imperial republicans.

delink-world-market.rationale: Development and trade policy lay outside the movement's concerns.

labor-aristocracy.rationale: Anti-clericalism took no position on the exploitation of rich-country workers.

freedom-to-discriminate.rationale: The 1905 law rests on state neutrality and equal treatment of all faiths, which fits equal-treatment rules; inferred, as it did not address private discrimination.

entrenched-bill-of-rights.rationale: The 1905 law guarantees freedom of conscience and worship as a basic right, and republican anti-clericals prized declared rights; inferred.

colonial-treaties-void.rationale: Anti-clericalism is a stance on clerical power and has no position on colonial treaties.

elective-rulers.rationale: Anti-clerical movements were mostly republican and opposed the alliance of throne and altar, so election over inheritance is inferred.

minority-veto.rationale: Republican anti-clericals legislated against the Church by majority vote, so a minority veto is rejected by inference.

resist-lawless-ruler.rationale: Adherents split between liberal constitutionalists and revolutionaries; the movement has no common doctrine of resistance.

parliament-supreme.rationale: French anti-clericals passed the Ferry laws and the 1905 law through parliament and opposed clerical and royalist rivals to it, so parliamentary supremacy is inferred.

animal-suffering-matters.rationale: The movement does not address animals.

animal-use-humane.rationale: The movement does not address animal use.

noblesse-oblige.rationale: Anti-clericals wanted charity and welfare moved from church control to the state, though this is inferred and aristocratic duty was not a theme.

withdraw-from-politics.rationale: Anti-clericalism is an active political campaign, so withdrawal contradicts it; inferred, not documented.

mass-culture-pacifies.rationale: Anti-clericals criticised the Church for keeping people docile, but have no general theory about mass culture or media.

ruling-class-consent.rationale: Not addressed; adherents range from liberals to socialists with differing views.

world-economy-extracts-surplus.rationale: Not addressed; the movement has no economic doctrine and its supporters spanned liberal to socialist views.

indigenous-political-leadership.rationale: Republican anti-clericals favoured equal citizenship, not rule by descent groups; inferred from the universal-citizen ideal.

antifascism-founding-value.rationale: The movement predates fascism and is split on constitutional values beyond church-state separation, so no single answer is documented.

totalitarianisms-equivalent.rationale: Not addressed; anti-clericals include liberals and socialists who answer differently.

slavery-not-civil-war-cause.rationale: Republican and liberal anti-clericals would be expected to accept the mainstream account that slavery was the cause; inferred, with no documented stance.

preserve-contested-monuments.rationale: Anti-clericals removed religious symbols from public space, yet a position on monuments of condemned figures is not documented.

institutions-fit-civilization.rationale: Republican anti-clericals held that secular state institutions suit all societies; inferred from their universalist Enlightenment outlook.

military-guardian-role.rationale: French republicans insisted on civilian control and opposed a politically powerful army tied to the Church after the Dreyfus affair; inferred.

filial-duty.rationale: Anti-clericalism is about clerical power, not family duties; adherents range widely.

office-by-exam.rationale: Anti-clericals opposed church patronage and favoured republican, merit-based public service; inferred, not stated.

foreign-takeover-block.rationale: Outside the movement's concern with the church; adherents were split.

no-fault-divorce.rationale: Republican anti-clericals secularised marriage and backed civil divorce against Church law; inferred from that, not sourced directly.

recallable-delegates.rationale: The movement had no position on binding delegates; supporters ran from liberals to radicals.

individual-pension-accounts.rationale: No position on pensions; supporters spanned liberal and socialist views.

land-use-tenure.rationale: Anti-clericals mainly wanted church land seized, but liberal strands defended individual property; communal tenure was not their aim.

budget-needs-parliament.rationale: The 1905 law ended state funding of worship and republicans held to parliamentary control of public money; inferred.

single-official-language.rationale: The Ferry schools taught in French and made it the common medium of public education; inferred beyond that.

foreign-land-ownership.rationale: No position on foreign land ownership; outside the movement's concern.

disparate-impact-discrimination.rationale: The movement had no stance on racial outcomes.

arm-foreign-insurgents.rationale: No position on arming foreign insurgents; supporters divided.

intervene-in-bloc.rationale: Republican anti-clericalism stressed state sovereignty and secular self-rule, so imposed intervention is inferred to be disfavoured.

corporate-influence.rationale: The movement concerns clerical power, not corporate money; supporters spanned liberal to socialist.

restrict-foreign-funding.rationale: Anti-clericals feared foreign influence from Rome but took no stated position on foreign funding of NGOs or universities.

pronatalist-incentives.rationale: Birth policy lay outside the concerns of anti-clericalism.

residents-only-property.rationale: Property purchase rules were not an anti-clerical issue beyond church property.

job-guarantee.rationale: Employment policy was not part of the movement's programme.

democratic-peace.rationale: Republican anti-clericals often held liberal internationalist views but the movement has no line on democracy and war.

no-duty-to-obey.rationale: Anti-clericals sought to subject clergy to state law and the 1905 law punished clergy who urged resistance to it, but no general view on a duty to obey follows.

non-intervention.rationale: The movement has no line on foreign intervention.

industrial-unions.rationale: Union structure was not an anti-clerical question.

minority-conspiracy.rationale: Anti-clericals attacked clerical power, not minorities; the Jesuit-plot rhetoric targeted an institution; inferred.

abolish-legal-marriage.rationale: State civil marriage replaced church marriage in anti-clerical reforms, so they favoured the state institution, not its abolition; inferred.

public-access-to-information.rationale: Anti-clericals wanted transparency about church affairs but the movement has no general view on access to records.

local-production.rationale: Local production lay outside the movement's concerns.

informal-organisation.rationale: Anti-clerical politics worked through parties, lodges and leagues, and the ideology has no organisational doctrine.

national-law-over-international.rationale: The movement sought church-state separation under national law, but it has no stated view on international courts.

religious-nation.rationale: Separation of churches and state, secular schools and freedom of conscience mean nationality does not depend on religion.

missingStatements.text: The state should confiscate church property and use it for public purposes.
missingStatements.rationale: Nationalising church lands and buildings (France 1789, Spain's Mendizabal, Mexico's Juarez) is a defining anti-clerical measure; no current statement asks about it directly.

missingStatements.text: Religious orders should be barred from teaching in schools.
missingStatements.rationale: The Ferry laws barred members of congregations from public teaching and France's 1904 law ended congregational teaching entirely.

missingStatements.text: Clergy should be forbidden from political activity in places of worship.
missingStatements.rationale: The 1905 law banned political meetings in places of worship and punished clergy who urged resistance to law or defamed officials.

notes: Anti-clericalism ranges from liberal secularism (freedom of conscience, 1905 law) to state campaigns of repression (Calles in Mexico, Cuba), and violent episodes in revolutionary France and Spain. The profile follows the republican mainstream, and strands such as Marxist atheism or violent suppression would answer several questions differently.
